title: Liquid Metal Coatings on Lithium Metal Anodes Protect Against Capacity Fade: A Cryo Electron Microscopy Study
content: With the advancements in portable electronics, from vehicles to communication devices, the need for long-lived, high-energy density storage systems is crucial [1]. Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) with metal oxide cathodes and graphite anodes are currently the leading technology for commercial energy storage devices but suffer from a limited theoretical energy density [2]. Lithium metal anodes are a higher energy density anode for next generation Li-oxygen and Li-sulfur due to their ultra-high theoretical capacity [3]. A major obstacle in implementing Li metal anodes is their reactivity. Detrimental reactions between the electrode and the electrolyte cause nonplanar Li growth that ultimately disconnects from the current collector decreasing the cell capacity or causing a short circuit [4]. The use of a liquid metal coating as a protective, artificial solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) aims to direct Li deposition and reduce the formation of SEI in abundance to extend the cycling lifespan [5]. There is still a lack of mechanistic understanding of how these liquid metal coatings contribute to improvement in cycling lifetime due to the challenge presented in the nanoscale characterization of site-specific chemistry in these systems. This work focuses on the use of cryogenic microscopy (cryo-EM) techniques to probe the delicate electrode-SEI-electrolyte interfaces of liquid metal (Ga, GaIn, and GaInSn) coated Li-metal electrodes to gain a mechanistic understanding of interfacial degradation and chemistry.
